newsitem.title: CHINA: Here are the key facts about China.
newsitem.headline: Here are the key facts about China.

text.p: Population: 1.2 billion at end 1995, the world's biggest, expected to reach 1.3 billion by the year 2000.
Area: 3.7 million sq miles (9.6 million sq km).

China's neighbours are Russia and Mongolia to the north: North Korea in the northeast: the former Soviet republics of Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan in the northwest: Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, Nepal and Bhutan to the west and southwest: and Burma, Laos and Vietnam to the south.
Capital: Beijing (old spelling Peking.)
Armed forces: Strategic -- at least 17 intercontinental, 70 intermediate range and 50 medium range ballistic missiles.

Total regular forces of the People's Liberation Army: about three million. Active about 2.3 million, reserves about 1.2 million. Tanks about 9,200, artillery 14,500. Air force: around 4,500 fighters and ground attack aircraft, about 420 light and medium bombers. Navy: About 60 destroyers and frigates, about 112 diesel submarines and 5 nuclear. (source diplomatic and published Western estimates)
Economy:

Gross Domestic Product for 1996 estimated at 6.78 trillion yuan, up 9.7 percent compared with 1995. Annual per capita income of urban residents in 1996 was 4,380 yuan ($527), for rural residents 1,900 yuan ($228). Some 75 percent of the population lives in rural areas.
Grain output for 1996 estimated at a record 480 million tonnes up from 466 million tonnes in 1995.
Retail price inflation in 1996 fell to 6.1 percent, from 14.8 percent in 1995.

Total trade in 1996 estimated at $289.9 billion, up 3.3 percent from 1995. Its surplus was $12.24 billion, down from $16 billion in 1995. Main trading partners were Hong Kong, the United States and Japan.
Total foreign investment in 1996 was estimated at $48 billion.
Total foreign reserves were $105 billion at end-1996.
Currency: One U.S. dollar was worth 8.29 yuan at end-1996, down from 8.3 yuan at end-1995.

Modern history: China's last imperial dynasty, the Qing, fell in 1911 to republican forces. In the 1920s, China became increasingly split between the Nationalists led by Chiang Kai-shek and the Communists. Mao Zedong proclaimed the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949 after a civil war that ended with the bulk of Chiang's army fleeing to Taiwan.

China was closely allied to the Soviet Union in the first years after the revolution and modelled itself on Stalin's centralised system. Ideological and foreign policy arguments broke out and the two communist giants split bitterly in the early 1960s. Clashes broke out along their common frontier.
India and China fought a brief war along their Himalayan border in 1962.
Mao's ambitious "great leap forward", begun in 1958, brought economic disaster and contributed to serious famine in 1960 that killed about 28 million.

In 1966, Chairman Mao launched the Cultural Revolution during which President Liu Shaoqi and China's present leader, Deng Xiaoping, were branded "capitalist roaders". Liu died in prison, Deng was cast into political exile. Millions of ordinary people had their lives scarred forever by the decade of trauma.
In 1971, a planned coup led by Defence Minister Lin Biao was foiled and Lin was killed when his plane crashed in Mongolia during an escape attempt to the Soviet Union.
Despite domestic turmoil, China -- with few friends to its name -- began to mend its bridges with the non-communist world while relations with the Soviet bloc remained hostile.

China was admitted to the United Nations in 1971 and President Richard Nixon became the first U.S. leader to visit communist China in 1972. Relations with Washington were normalised in 1979 and ties have improved since then despite quarrels over Taiwan, trade and human rights issues.

The year 1976 was historic for China. A massive earthquake killed over 250,000 people in the north. Mao died and the radical "gang of four" led by Mao's widow Jiang Qing were arrested and thrown into prison.
Hua Guofeng succeeded Mao as party leader but his failure to challenge Maoist orthodoxy came under attack from Deng who had emerged from a second period of political disgrace.

Deng launched China's ambitious programme of economic reforms in late 1978 and soon installed his proteges in power. Zhao Ziyang replaced Hua as premier in 1980. A year later Hu Yaobang took the party leadership but was himself ousted by hardliners in January, 1987, after nationwide demonstrations by students calling for democracy and freedom.
Zhao was named acting party leader and confirmed in the post at a party congress in November, 1987, when Deng engineered a mass retirement of many elderly, hardline party veterans.
Li Peng, a Soviet-trained technocrat and a relatively youthful 59-year-old, became premier.
In the summer of 1988, China began sliding into economic chaos with bank runs and panic buying triggered by rising inflation that peaked at more than 30 per cent in cities.
Authorities responded in October by tightening the screws on the economy to cool growth and lower inflation.
1989 was a year of violence, starting with the suppression of demonstrations in Tibet and the subsequent declaration of martial law there on March 7.

Beijing university students wrote posters denouncing Deng and Premier Li by name and criticising them and the Communist Party for corruption and use of autocratic and arbitrary power. The students demanded democratic change.

Martial law was declared on May 20 and army tanks and troops crushed the student-led protests on June 4, killing hundreds of people. Zhao Ziyang was purged as Communist Party General Secretary and replaced by Jiang Zemin.
Many Western nations clamped economic, military and political sanctions on China, adding to its economic woes.
Deng resigned as head of the party's Central Military Commission in November 1989 to try to bolster the position of Jiang, his third designated successor.
By early 1991, economic sanctions against Beijing had largely been lifted, new loans had been extended and western leaders were once again beating a path to China's door.
However, the economy began to slow in 1991 amid signs top leaders were nervous about new reforms.

Early in 1992, Deng, now 87, revealed he remained China's paramount leader, albeit without a formal title, by making a high-profile tour of the reform test-tube town of Shenzhen that neighbours Hong Kong and kick-starting an economic boom.
In 1992, he used that momentum to sweep the remaining old guard from the party central central committee at a crucial congress, endorsed his economic reforms and boosted Jiang.

The economy flourished, notching up the world's fastest growth rates in 1993 and 1994 but triggering a surge in inflation to a communist-era high of 21.7 percent in 1994 and prompting a draconian credit squeeze in the middle of the year.
It maintained its momentum in 1995, powered by the booming capitalist-style export industries of the south and coast and responding slowly to efforts to restrain overheating.
China pressed ahead with financial reforms, regulating its dual-track exchange rate and welcoming foreign banks.

Commodities futures were born along with two stock markets, in Shanghai and Shenzhen, although rampant speculation forced securities regulators to close many markets and to ban contracts ranging from grains, red beans and treasury bill futures.
China's leaders have tiptoed around the reform of lumbering state industry, backbone of the socialist economy, that is held back by terrible problems of inefficiency and bad management.
At end-1996, nearly two-thirds of the companies lost money, and were propped up by huge state subsidies and bad debt, throwing state banks and the budget off balance.
While the government has pledged to fix the system, many economists believe the problems will defy easy answers.
China's communist leaders were badly shaken by the collapse of the Soviet Union and at home stability was their watchword.
However, in 1996 they made clear that stability stopped short of allowing Taiwan, which Beijing regards as a renegade province, to toy with independence.

China backed the message with intimidating war games off Taiwan after its President Lee Teng-hui made a landmark private visit to the United States, and tried to influence his vote bank in the island's first direct presidential elections in 1996.
It has never ruled out force to recover Taiwan, whether it will make good that threat remains to be seen.

In mid-February 1997, strong rumours surfaced about the health of Deng. Reports that he was seriously ill gained strength after President Jiang and Premier Li cut short provincial trips to return to Beijing.
Late on Wednesday, February 19, 1997, Deng dies aged 92. He died of respiratory failure after he did not respond to emergency treatment, Xinhua news agency reported.
